tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
# @entirehq mention watcher

Someone replies to `@entirehq` on X. You find out four hours later, because
nobody had that search tab open.

This closes that gap. A daemon polls the live `@entirehq` search every five
minutes and posts every new mention, reply, and quote tweet to Slack.

```
@somedev replied to @entirehq
> hey @entirehq does this work with self-hosted runners?
View on X · reply · Aug 18 at 5:17 PM
```

It runs as a launchd agent — at login, across reboots, restarted if it dies,
independent of whether Claude Code is open. Zero tokens: a plain Node process
posting to a webhook, not an agent.

## Setup

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env       # fill in the five values below
npm run check              # one live scrape, printed, notifies nobody
npm run install-agent      # install + start the daemon
```

| Variable | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` | browserbase.com → Settings |
| `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID` | same page |
| `X_AUTH_TOKEN` | logged-in x.com tab → DevTools → Application → Cookies → `auth_token` |
| `X_CSRF_TOKEN` | same place → `ct0` |
| `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | api.slack.com/apps → your app → Incoming Webhooks |

Optional: `X_WATCH_POLL_MS` (`300000`), `X_SEARCH_QUERY` (`@entirehq`),
`X_OWN_HANDLE` (`entirehq`).

Config is read once at boot — after editing `.env`, re-run `install-agent`.

**Why cookies, not the X API.** Live search is login-gated, and API v2's
recent-search endpoint needs a paid tier (~$200/mo). Two cookies cost nothing
and last months; when they expire the watcher says so in Slack rather than
returning nothing, which would read as "nobody is mentioning us."

## How it works

```
launchd (RunAtLoad, KeepAlive) → watch.mjs
   ↓
   scrape ──→ parse ──→ filter ──→ diff ──→ post to Slack
   Browserbase   X's own    drop our    seen-id     Block Kit
   + Playwright  JSON       own posts,  store       webhook
                 (DOM        label
                  fallback)  kind
   ↓
   sleep 5m, repeat
```

- **Claude Code's hooks are a fallback.** `SessionStart`/`SessionEnd` run a
  session-scoped watcher only when no agent is installed for this project. With
  the agent installed they stand down, so notifications never double up.
- **Slack is the only channel.** Nothing prints to your terminal; diagnostics
  go to `.claude/entirehq-watcher/watch.log` — including when Slack is the
  thing that's broken.
- **It reads X's JSON, not the page.** Playwright intercepts the
  `SearchTimeline` response instead of scraping `data-testid` attributes X
  rotates at will. Reply/quote classification uses real fields
  (`in_reply_to_status_id`, `is_quote_status`). DOM extraction is a labelled
  fallback.
- **Seen only once Slack accepts it.** Marking a failed post as seen would drop
  that mention permanently and silently; a failure costs one duplicate attempt
  next poll instead.
- **The first run notifies nobody.** It baselines whatever is already on the
  page, or day one dumps every existing mention into Slack.
- **It won't shut up about being broken.** Expired cookies, scrapes stuck at
  the 30-minute backoff cap, and three consecutive empty polls each fire
  exactly one Slack alert, deduped through the store so restarts don't
  re-alarm.

## Known limitations

- **One page per poll** — no scrolling, so roughly X's first ~20 results.
  Heavier bursts overflow; the watcher logs a note when a poll comes back that
  full. Shorter `X_WATCH_POLL_MS` reduces the risk at the cost of more sessions.
- **`X_OWN_HANDLE` suppresses one account** — teammates' personal replies do
  notify.
- **One agent per machine** — the launchd label is fixed. A second checkout
  sees the plist names a different project and falls back to its hooks.
- **Automated browsing is contrary to X's ToS** — accepted knowingly, for one
  account's own brand mentions at low volume.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run install-agent` | Install and start the daemon (idempotent) |
| `npm run uninstall-agent` | Stop and remove it; hooks take over again |
| `npm run check` | One live scrape, dry-run, notifies nobody |
| `npm test` | 97 tests: config, both parsers, filter, store, notifiers, launchd |
| `tail -f .claude/entirehq-watcher/watch.log` | What the daemon is doing |

One Browserbase session per poll — 288/day at the default, now continuous
rather than only while an editor is open.

## Layout

| Path | |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/config.mjs` | Loads and validates `.env`; native `loadEnvFile` |
| `scripts/x-scrape.mjs` | Browserbase session, cookies, JSON interception, DOM fallback |
| `scripts/parse.mjs` | Both payload shapes → normalized records. Pure |
| `scripts/filter.mjs` | Drops our own posts, labels mention/reply/quote. Pure |
| `scripts/store.mjs` | Seen-id cache, 500-id cap, baseline and alert flags |
| `scripts/notify-slack.mjs` | Block Kit payload, webhook POST, one retry |
| `scripts/notify-terminal.mjs` | ANSI output — `check.mjs` only |
| `scripts/watch.mjs` | The poll loop: backoff, alerting, logging, shutdown |
| `scripts/launchd.mjs` | Plist generation, per-project ownership check. Pure |
| `scripts/install-agent.mjs` / `uninstall-agent.mjs` | Daemon lifecycle |
| `scripts/hook-start.mjs` / `hook-stop.mjs` | Session-scoped fallback |

Node ≥ 20.12, ESM, two runtime dependencies (`@browserbasehq/sdk`,
`playwright-core`), zero test dependencies — the suite is `node:test`.
`parse`, `filter`, `store`, and `launchd` are pure functions, which is why the
logic is testable without a network.

## How this was built

Spec → plan → ten TDD tasks, each implemented by one agent and reviewed by
another. Design doc and plan are in `docs/superpowers/`, committed before any
code was written.

Review caught six defects that originated in the plan itself — a `node --test`
invocation that silently exits 1 on Node 24+, a Browserbase session leaked on
every connect failure (billable), and a store that marked a batch seen *before*
announcing it, losing the remainder if killed mid-batch.

The first live run exposed the one thing no test could: the watcher had never
actually run. It only existed while a Claude Code session was open — which is
what the launchd agent replaced.

content.text: I have the full picture. The repo has no scoring concept yet, so this trail introduces one. Two decisions are genuinely yours before I build.

questions.question: The trail title says "if an employee is tagged" but the body says "if [employees] tweet about us." Which signal should drive the score?

options.label: Both, scored oppositely (Recommended)
options.description: Employee-AUTHORED tweets score DOWN (internal amplification, likely a reply to an inbound tag we already saw). Tweets by outsiders that TAG an employee score UP (someone is reaching a specific person at Entire). Covers the title and the body.

options.label: Employee-authored only
options.description: Only score down tweets written by the six employee handles. Ignore whether a tweet tags an employee. Simpler, matches the trail body literally.

options.label: Employee-tagged only
options.description: Only score up tweets that tag one of the six handles. Tweets authored by employees score normally. Matches the trail title literally.

questions.question: What should the score actually change in Slack?

options.label: Label + badge only (Recommended)
options.description: Every mention still posts, in chronological order as today. The Slack message carries the score and a reason line ("Entire team" / "tags @lizziepika"). Nothing is hidden. Smallest blast radius, matches "take note of it."
options.preview:
*@lizziepika* replied to @entirehq
>yep, self-hosted runners work out of the box

View on X · reply · Entire team · score 20 · Sep 14

options.label: Label + announce high scores first
options.description: Same badges, but within a poll batch the highest-scoring fresh tweets post to Slack before low scorers. Breaks the current oldest-first ordering.
options.preview:
score 85  @randodev  ← posts first
score 20  @lizziepika ← posts second
(even though @lizziepika tweeted earlier)

options.label: Label + mute low scores
options.description: Employee-authored tweets stop posting to Slack entirely; they are marked seen and logged to watch.log only. Quietest channel, but you lose sight of team replies.
options.preview:

Worth noting from `entire agent-help enable`: bare `--force` is **interactive**. It'll prompt you for which agents to set up, and if that prompt got dismissed, nothing gets written. The non-interactive form avoids that:

```
! entire enable --force --agent claude-code
```

`--agent` explicitly "enables non-interactive mode" per the CLI's own help, so it targets Claude Code's hooks and skips the picker.

Two flags to be deliberate about, since this repo is public:

- Don't pass `-y`/`--yes`. It accepts every default at once, including telemetry.
- `--skip-push-sessions` exists if you want to be sure this run doesn't turn on automatic session-log pushing. That's the public-repo concern I raised earlier and still haven't walked you through, so if you'd rather not decide it right now, adding that flag keeps the status quo.

So the conservative version:

```
! entire enable --force --agent claude-code --skip-push-sessions
```

+// Note what this deliberately does NOT do: a tweet that *tags* an employee

+// Rendered by both notifiers. Lives here so the two never drift apart.
+// X handles are case-insensitive and users write them with and without the
+// leading @, so every comparison happens on a normalized form. Returns a Set
+// because the caller checks membership once per tweet per poll.
+// Accepts either an already-normalized Set (the hot path, built once per poll)
+// or a raw array, so callers are not forced to remember which they hold.
+  if (employees === undefined || employees === null) return DEFAULT_EMPLOYEE_SET;

1	# @entirehq mention watcher
2	
3	Someone replies to `@entirehq` on X. You find out four hours later, because
4	nobody had that search tab open.
5	
6	This closes that gap. A daemon polls the live `@entirehq` search every five
7	minutes and posts every new mention, reply, and quote tweet to Slack.
8	
9	```
10	@somedev replied to @entirehq
11	> hey @entirehq does this work with self-hosted runners?
12	View on X · reply · Aug 18 at 5:17 PM
13	```
14	
15	It runs as a launchd agent — at login, across reboots, restarted if it dies,
16	independent of whether Claude Code is open. Zero tokens: a plain Node process
17	posting to a webhook, not an agent.
18	
19	## Setup
20	
21	```bash
22	npm install
23	cp .env.example .env       # fill in the five values below
24	npm run check              # one live scrape, printed, notifies nobody
25	npm run install-agent      # install + start the daemon
26	```
27	
28	| Variable | Where it comes from |
29	| --- | --- |
30	| `BROWSERBASE_API_KEY` | browserbase.com → Settings |
31	| `BROWSERBASE_PROJECT_ID` | same page |
32	| `X_AUTH_TOKEN` | logged-in x.com tab → DevTools → Application → Cookies → `auth_token` |
33	| `X_CSRF_TOKEN` | same place → `ct0` |
34	| `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | api.slack.com/apps → your app → Incoming Webhooks |
35	
36	Optional: `X_WATCH_POLL_MS` (`300000`), `X_SEARCH_QUERY` (`@entirehq`),
37	`X_OWN_HANDLE` (`entirehq`), `X_EMPLOYEE_HANDLES` (the six handles in
38	`scripts/score.mjs`).
39	
40	Config is read once at boot — after editing `.env`, re-run `install-agent`.
41	
42	**Why cookies, not the X API.** Live search is login-gated, and API v2's
43	recent-search endpoint needs a paid tier (~$200/mo). Two cookies cost nothing
44	and last months; when they expire the watcher says so in Slack rather than
45	returning nothing, which would read as "nobody is mentioning us."
46	
47	## How it works
48	
49	```
50	launchd (RunAtLoad, KeepAlive) → watch.mjs
51	   ↓
52	   scrape ──→ parse ──→ filter ──→ diff ──→ post to Slack
53	   Browserbase   X's own    drop our    seen-id     Block Kit
54	   + Playwright  JSON       own posts,  store       webhook
55	                 (DOM        label
56	                  fallback)  kind, score
57	   ↓
58	   sleep 5m, repeat
59	```
60	
61	- **Claude Code's hooks are a fallback.** `SessionStart`/`SessionEnd` run a
62	  session-scoped watcher only when no agent is installed for this project. With
63	  the agent installed they stand down, so notifications never double up.
64	- **Slack is the only channel.** Nothing prints to your terminal; diagnostics
65	  go to `.claude/entirehq-watcher/watch.log` — including when Slack is the
66	  thing that's broken.
67	- **It reads X's JSON, not the page.** Playwright intercepts the
68	  `SearchTimeline` response instead of scraping `data-testid` attributes X
69	  rotates at will. Reply/quote classification uses real fields
70	  (`in_reply_to_status_id`, `is_quote_status`). DOM extraction is a labelled
71	  fallback.
72	- **A teammate's post is not the same signal as a stranger's.** Posts authored
73	  by the Entire team (`@blackgirlbytes`, `@lizziepika`, `@evisdrenova`,
74	  `@ashtom`, `@jkcso`, `@HaimantikaM`) score 20; everyone else scores 60. They
75	  are still announced, in the same chronological order, but badged `Entire
76	  team` in the Slack context line and in the notification preview, so team
77	  chatter never reads as fresh outside interest. Only authorship moves the
78	  number: a stranger *tagging* a teammate scores like any other stranger.
79	- **Seen only once Slack accepts it.** Marking a failed post as seen would drop
80	  that mention permanently and silently; a failure costs one duplicate attempt
81	  next poll instead.
82	- **The first run notifies nobody.** It baselines whatever is already on the
83	  page, or day one dumps every existing mention into Slack.
84	- **It won't shut up about being broken.** Expired cookies, scrapes stuck at
85	  the 30-minute backoff cap, and three consecutive empty polls each fire
86	  exactly one Slack alert, deduped through the store so restarts don't
87	  re-alarm.
88	
89	## Known limitations
90	
91	- **One page per poll** — no scrolling, so roughly X's first ~20 results.
92	  Heavier bursts overflow; the watcher logs a note when a poll comes back that
93	  full. Shorter `X_WATCH_POLL_MS` reduces the risk at the cost of more sessions.
94	- **`X_OWN_HANDLE` suppresses one account** — teammates' personal replies do
95	  notify.
96	- **One agent per machine** — the launchd label is fixed. A second checkout
97	  sees the plist names a different project and falls back to its hooks.
98	- **Automated browsing is contrary to X's ToS** — accepted knowingly, for one
99	  account's own brand mentions at low volume.
100	
101	## Commands
102	
103	| Command | What it does |
104	| --- | --- |
105	| `npm run install-agent` | Install and start the daemon (idempotent) |
106	| `npm run uninstall-agent` | Stop and remove it; hooks take over again |
107	| `npm run check` | One live scrape, dry-run, notifies nobody |
108	| `npm test` | 134 tests: config, both parsers, filter, score, store, notifiers, launchd |
109	| `tail -f .claude/entirehq-watcher/watch.log` | What the daemon is doing |
110	
111	One Browserbase session per poll — 288/day at the default, now continuous
112	rather than only while an editor is open.
113	
114	## Layout
115	
116	| Path | |
117	| --- | --- |
118	| `scripts/config.mjs` | Loads and validates `.env`; native `loadEnvFile` |
119	| `scripts/x-scrape.mjs` | Browserbase session, cookies, JSON interception, DOM fallback |
120	| `scripts/parse.mjs` | Both payload shapes → normalized records. Pure |
121	| `scripts/filter.mjs` | Drops our own posts, labels mention/reply/quote, attaches the score. Pure |
122	| `scripts/score.mjs` | Employee roster and the scoring rule. Pure |
123	| `scripts/store.mjs` | Seen-id cache, 500-id cap, baseline and alert flags |
124	| `scripts/notify-slack.mjs` | Block Kit payload, webhook POST, one retry |
125	| `scripts/notify-terminal.mjs` | ANSI output — `check.mjs` only |
126	| `scripts/watch.mjs` | The poll loop: backoff, alerting, logging, shutdown |
127	| `scripts/launchd.mjs` | Plist generation, per-project ownership check. Pure |
128	| `scripts/install-agent.mjs` / `uninstall-agent.mjs` | Daemon lifecycle |
129	| `scripts/hook-start.mjs` / `hook-stop.mjs` | Session-scoped fallback |
130	
131	Node ≥ 20.12, ESM, two runtime dependencies (`@browserbasehq/sdk`,
132	`playwright-core`), zero test dependencies — the suite is `node:test`.
133	`parse`, `filter`, `score`, `store`, and `launchd` are pure functions, which is
134	why the logic is testable without a network.
135	
136	## How this was built
137	
138	Spec → plan → ten TDD tasks, each implemented by one agent and reviewed by
139	another. Design doc and plan are in `docs/superpowers/`, committed before any
140	code was written.
141	
142	Review caught six defects that originated in the plan itself — a `node --test`
143	invocation that silently exits 1 on Node 24+, a Browserbase session leaked on
144	every connect failure (billable), and a store that marked a batch seen *before*
145	announcing it, losing the remainder if killed mid-batch.
146	
147	The first live run exposed the one thing no test could: the watcher had never
148	actually run. It only existed while a Claude Code session was open — which is
149	what the launchd agent replaced.

Done. Trail #3 is implemented and verified.

## Outcome

Employee-authored mentions now score 20 instead of 60 and carry an `Entire team` badge. Nothing is hidden, nothing is reordered, exactly as you specified.

**New:** `scripts/score.mjs`, a pure module holding the roster and the one scoring rule. `scripts/filter.mjs` attaches `score` and `isEmployee` to every record; both notifiers render them; `config.mjs` exposes the roster with an `X_EMPLOYEE_HANDLES` override so adding a teammate isn't a code change.

## Verification

`npm test`: **134 passing, 0 failing** (was 97, so 37 new). `node --check` clean across every script and test.

Unit tests alone wouldn't prove the wiring, so I also ran the real pipeline against the repo's own fixture, no network:

```
roster from loadConfig: blackgirlbytes, lizziepika, evisdrenova, ashtom, jkcso, haimantikam
parsed from fixture: 4 tweets → 3 announced   (@entirehq's own post dropped)

@lizziepika mentioned @entirehq (Entire team)
  · mention · Entire team · score 20
@oldshape replied to @entirehq
  · reply · score 60
@QuoteFan quoted @entirehq
  · quote · score 60
```

Three details worth knowing I made calls on:

- **The badge reaches the notification fallback**, not just the block body. On mobile the popup is all you see, so a badge only in the context line would be invisible where it matters most.
- **The context line is assembled from parts**, so a record without a score renders no segment rather than `score undefined`. Pinned by a test, along with score `0` not being swallowed as falsy.
- **A stranger tagging a teammate scores 60**, like any stranger. Your trail *title* says "tagged" while the body says employees tweeting, and you chose authorship-only. There's a test named for that so the next person doesn't quietly reinterpret it.

`npm run check` against live X is the one thing I could not run: it needs Browserbase credentials and a real scrape. The fixture run above covers the same code path minus the network.

## Not committed, not pushed

No authorization for either, so the work is sitting in the tree: 10 modified files plus 2 new ones. Two unrelated changes are mixed in that I'd keep out of a scoring commit:

- `.claude/settings.json`, the retired deny rule `entire doctor` removed
- `.entire/settings.json`, now carrying `"push_sessions": false` from the `--skip-push-sessions` flag

That second one is still the open question from earlier. It's a **tracked** file, so committing it publishes that choice, and it's the opposite of the `true` your CLAUDE.md wants. Public repo, so I'm still not touching it without walking you through what session refs carry. Say the word and we'll settle it.

Entire is healthy: hooks `OK`, session `bfb8143d` live. `Checkpoints: 0` is expected, since checkpoints are minted on commit.

Good serve to get the hooks sorted first. Tracking was the net, and we're playing on the right side of it now.

input.command:
git commit -F - <<'EOF'
feat: score mentions lower when an Entire teammate is the author

A post from the Entire team is usually the company talking to itself: a
teammate answering an inbound tag we were already notified about, or
amplifying something we shipped. Worth recording, but it is not an outsider
raising something unprompted, and a channel that presents both identically
teaches you to skim past both.

Every mention now carries a score. Posts authored by the team score 20;
everyone else scores 60. Teammates are still announced, still in
chronological order, but badged "Entire team" in the Slack context line and
in the notification fallback, which is all a phone shows.

Only authorship moves the number. A stranger tagging a teammate scores like
any other stranger, and there is a test named for that so the rule does not
get quietly reinterpreted later.

The roster lives in employees.csv, not in code: one handle per line, @
optional, # for comments, anything after the first comma a free-text note. A
one-column file is just a plain list, so a .txt of handles works verbatim.
X_EMPLOYEE_HANDLES overrides the file for a one-off. An empty or unreadable
file falls back to the built-in roster rather than silently un-badging the
whole team, and nothing in that path throws: mis-scoring one post is
recoverable, refusing to boot is not.

scoring lives in scripts/score.mjs as pure functions, so the rule, the roster
parser and the handle validation are all testable without a network.

Verified: 151 tests pass (was 97). Also ran the real parse -> filter -> Slack
payload path against the checked-in fixture, and confirmed that appending one
line to employees.csv moves that author from 60 to 20 with no code change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
echo "=== COMMITTED ===" && git log --oneline -2
